asBirthCard.p: This one has nothing to do with where the planets were when you were born. It comes from the date. Add up every digit of your birthday, keep adding the digits of the total while it's over 22, and yours lands on nineteen, which is The Sun. Nineteen is a one beside a nine, the first digit next to the last, and if you add them you get ten and then one again, so it's a number about starting over once a whole cycle has run its course. Just before it in the Majors is The Moon, the card of bad dreams and not being sure what's real. Straight after it is Judgement, where someone hears their name called and stands up. The Sun is the morning in between. Its planet is the Sun, which rules Leo and is exalted in Aries, and your own signs could be anything, but the date has given you that hot, direct energy anyway, the sort that isn't much interested in hiding.

Over a life it tends to show up as things coming clear. There'll be a murky stretch, a job you can't read or a relationship where nobody says what they mean, and then one morning it resolves and you can see the whole shape of it. Day to day you don't cope well with things left unsaid. If a friend's gone quiet on you, you ring and ask what's wrong, and you'd honestly prefer a hard answer to a week of guessing. At your cousin's engagement party, with everyone carefully avoiding the subject of the ex, you're the one who brings up the ex, kindly, and the room is quietly relieved. You're usually the adult the kids at a barbecue attach themselves to within ten minutes, and you don't mind at all. And a day indoors with the blinds down leaves you flat and a bit irritable by four o'clock, even when nothing's actually wrong.

Everyone talks about your warmth, and it's real, but the rarer thing is how well you come back. Most people with this card have had some bad nights, sometimes whole years of them, and what's unusual is that when it lifts, it properly lifts. I've seen a nineteen go through a divorce and a redundancy in the same year and be laughing at a friend's fortieth the following summer, and it wasn't an act. You're also good at making hard things plain. Your mum comes out of the specialist's room frightened and muddled, and you can tell her what was said in three sentences she can hold on to for the drive home. You'll do the same for a colleague who's walked out of a restructure meeting with no idea whether they still have a job.

Because your own bad patches clear, you half expect everyone else's to, and on roughly your timetable. A friend is still low six months after her dad died and you catch yourself suggesting a holiday, a run, a new haircut, anything to get her back out into the daylight. It comes from love, and it still lands as pressure, and after a while she may stop telling you how she really is. You can be blunt too, in a way that leaves people exposed. You say the true thing at dinner, and it is true, and your brother-in-law didn't need it said in front of his kids. Then you drive home fairly sure you did everyone a favour.

When something goes badly wrong, a nineteen's first move is to get brighter. The redundancy, the break-up, a parent's bad news, and within a day you've got a plan, a spreadsheet and a joke about it for the group chat. People are relieved, because you seem fine. About a week later the light goes out quite suddenly. You sleep till eleven, stop answering messages, and sit in the car outside the house for twenty minutes before going in. Because you're known as the bright one, the people around you don't really know what to do with this version, and a few take it personally, as if you've withdrawn something from them. What helps is plain and physical. Daylight on your face first thing, meals at proper times, and one friend you don't have to be funny for.

You want to be known completely and to know the other person just as completely, which sounds lovely and can be a lot for them. By the third date you've usually told them everything, the family stuff, the debt, the one who broke your heart, and then you're a bit hurt when they don't do the same. Quite often you fall for someone with a bit of The Moon about them, private, moody, hard to read, and spend years trying to get the curtains open. What tends to work is letting them keep one drawer shut. You're also generous with praise for a partner and oddly shy about asking whether they're actually happy with you. Ask anyway, in plain words, on an ordinary evening when nothing's wrong.

You tend to end up as the person who explains things at work, the one who runs the kick-off and writes the email people actually read. Jobs that are all back room, where you never meet the people it's for and nobody sees what you did, usually wear you down within a couple of years even when you're good at them. You're strongest at the start of something and at the moment a stuck project finally comes clear, and you tend to lose interest in the long middle where nothing much shows. That's worth knowing before you take the next role. You also take feedback very personally, both ways. A good review can carry you for months and a lukewarm one can put you off the whole place, so ask someone you trust for the plain version before the formal one lands.

At twenty a lot of nineteens are still living in the card before theirs. There's often an anxious, unsettled late adolescence, not sure what they're for, and they're surprised later to hear their card is The Sun at all. Somewhere in the late twenties things start to clear. By the mid-thirties there's usually a sense of having come out into the open, a job that fits, friends who like the real version of you, and the warmth people keep mentioning. That's also the decade the always-on problem sets in, being the bright one for everybody. The fifties tend to bring the Judgement side of the number, a kind of summing up. Nineteens at that age often get plainer and happier, care less who's watching, and turn out to be very good with younger people stuck in their own bad patch, because they remember theirs.

Once in the next few weeks, when someone you love is having a low day, go and sit with them for ten minutes and don't suggest anything. No walk, no plan, no bright side, no 'have you tried'. If they talk, listen. If they don't, that's fine too, put the kettle on and sit back down. You'll feel the urge to fix it about two minutes in. Notice where it sits in your body, leave it there, and stay for the rest of the ten minutes.
